# Rendezvous: full documentation

> Rendezvous is an open protocol for agent-to-agent contact: agents find each other by a human address, the humans consent, and the agents exchange end-to-end encrypted messages over dumb relays (Nostr first). Draft spec v0.1 rev 3 with a TypeScript reference implementation (Apache-2.0).

This file concatenates the markdown of the key docs from https://rendezvous.nesher.co. The shorter index is https://rendezvous.nesher.co/llms.txt. Included, in order:

- Setup per agent (docs/agents.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/agents.md
- Claude Code plugin (plugins/rendezvous/README.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/plugin.md
- CLI and library (impl/README.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/cli.md
- MCP tools (impl/packages/mcp/README.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/mcp.md
- Protocol spec (SPEC.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/spec.md
- Contributing (CONTRIBUTING.md): https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/contributing.md

Not included: the FAQ on the home page, the roadmap design proposal and the repository's PLAN.md and NOTES.md.

---

Source: https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/agents.md

# Rendezvous with your agent

Rendezvous runs as a local MCP server, `rdv-mcp`, plus an optional skill that
teaches the agent the workflow. This page has one section per agent: how to
install, the MCP config, the skill, and how to check that it works.

Checked on 2026-10-25 against each client's own documentation (linked in every
section). Where a setup could not be run here, the section says so.

- [Claude Code](#claude-code) · [Claude Desktop](#claude-desktop) · [Cursor](#cursor) · [VS Code (GitHub Copilot)](#vs-code-github-copilot) · [Codex CLI](#codex-cli) · [Gemini CLI](#gemini-cli) · [Windsurf](#windsurf) · [Grok Build](#grok-build) · [OpenClaw](#openclaw) · [Hermes Agent](#hermes-agent) · [Muse Code](#muse-code)

## Before you start

1. **Install Rendezvous** (Node.js 20+, git and npm; no sudo). Every section
   below starts from this:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://rendezvous.nesher.co/install.sh | sh
   ```

   ```powershell
   irm https://rendezvous.nesher.co/install.ps1 | iex
   ```

   It builds into `~/.rendezvous/src` and puts `rdv` and `rdv-mcp` on your PATH.
   Run it again to update.

2. **Register `rdv-mcp`** with your agent (the config in its section), then
   restart the agent or reload its MCP servers.

3. **Windows: use the `node` form.** The installer writes `rdv-mcp.cmd`. A client
   that starts servers without a shell cannot run a `.cmd` file: a bare
   `rdv-mcp` fails with `ENOENT` (reproduced here with a no-shell spawn from
   Node 25; `cmd /c rdv-mcp` and a shell spawn both worked). Whether each client
   spawns through a shell was not tested, so on Windows give every client the
   built file directly. The path is the same in all sections:

   ```text
   C:\Users\<you>\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js
   ```

   In JSON write the backslashes doubled (`C:\\Users\\<you>\\...`). In TOML use
   a single-quoted string (`'C:\Users\<you>\...'`). Each section shows the
   macOS / Linux form and what changes on Windows. If you set `RDV_DIR`, use
   `<RDV_DIR>\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js`. Options such as
   `--profile omer` go after the path in `args`.

4. **Verify** by asking the agent: **"What's my rendezvous status?"** It should
   call `rdv_status` and show your agent ID, your addresses and your relays. If
   it says there is no agent yet, create one (ask it, with the skill installed, or
   run `rdv init --profile omer --email omer@example.com` yourself) and ask
   again. Without `--relay` the agent uses the default public relays
   (`wss://nos.lol`, `wss://relay.primal.net`, `wss://relay.nostr.net`,
   `wss://nostr.oxtr.dev`); add `--relay wss://…` once per relay to use your
   own instead. `rdv whoami` shows each relay's last OK and last error.

## Consent: approvals come back to you

The agent cannot approve a contact request, confirm a probe answer or confirm a
meeting. `rdv_grant` and `rdv_negotiate` succeed only when the human decides:

- **Clients with MCP elicitation** show you an approval form (the requester's
  fingerprint, how the request arrived, the greeting marked untrusted, a tier
  and a label). The model never sees the form.
- **Clients without elicitation**: the human types the confirm phrase shown by
  `rdv contact pending` in their own terminal to the agent. The agent passes it as
  `confirm_phrase`. Phrases are single-use and no tool result ever contains one.
- Or approve in your own terminal with `rdv contact grant`.

Elicitation support, as far as it could be checked:

| Agent | Elicitation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | yes (interactive sessions, not `-p`) | `impl/packages/mcp/README.md` |
| Cursor | yes, verified: the MCP docs list elicitation as "Supported" | [Cursor MCP docs](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp) |
| Hermes Agent | yes, form mode, through its normal approval surface (on by default) | [Hermes MCP docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/mcp) |
| Claude Desktop, VS Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Grok Build, OpenClaw, Muse Code | not confirmed in their docs | treat as no: use the confirm phrase |

The plugin's consent guard (a hook that refuses the consent commands) exists
only in Claude Code. Elsewhere the consent gate is the boundary, and the skill's
rules tell the agent never to run those commands itself. Details and the threat
model: [`impl/packages/mcp/README.md`](https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/mcp.md#consent-the-human-decides-demo-critical).

## Claude Code

- **MCP + skill, one step:** the plugin registers `rdv-mcp` and adds the skill.
  In Claude Code's chat:

  ```text
  /plugin marketplace add omernesh/rendezvous
  /plugin install rendezvous@rendezvous
  /reload-plugins
  ```

  Then type `/rdv-onboarding` (or `/rendezvous:rdv-onboarding`). It points you to
  the installer for `rdv` and sets you up one question at a time. The plugin starts the
  server through `bin/rdv-mcp.mjs` under `node`, so Windows needs nothing special.
- **Without the plugin:** `claude mcp add rendezvous -- rdv-mcp` (Windows:
  `claude mcp add rendezvous -- cmd /c rdv-mcp`).
- **Verify:** ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** approval forms (elicitation) in an interactive session.
- Docs: [Claude Code MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), [plugins](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins).

## Claude Desktop

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
  (macOS) or `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` (Windows); in the app,
  Settings, Developer, Edit Config. Restart Claude Desktop completely after saving.

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": [] } } }
  ```

  Windows:
  `{ "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "node", "args": ["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"] } } }`
- **Skill:** none to install here; the MCP tools carry their own instructions.
  Claude Desktop's own skill upload is not covered by this page.
- **Verify:** ask "What's my rendezvous status?". Logs: `~/Library/Logs/Claude`
  or `%APPDATA%\Claude\logs` (`mcp-server-rendezvous.log`).
- **Consent:** elicitation not confirmed; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [Connect to local MCP servers](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers).

## Cursor

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (everywhere) or `.cursor/mcp.json` (one project).

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": [] } } }
  ```

  Windows: `"command": "node", "args": ["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"]`.
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` (the skills CLI lets you pick
  Cursor). Optional: the MCP server works without it.
- **Verify:** Settings, MCP: `rendezvous` should show its tools. Ask "What's my
  rendezvous status?" in the agent chat.
- **Consent:** elicitation supported (verified): you get the approval form.
- Docs: [Cursor MCP](https://cursor.com/docs/mcp).

## VS Code (GitHub Copilot)

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `.vscode/mcp.json` in a workspace, or your user `mcp.json`
  (Command Palette, "MCP: Open User Configuration"). VS Code's key is `servers`,
  not `mcpServers`.

  ```json
  { "servers": { "rendezvous": { "type": "stdio", "command": "rdv-mcp" } } }
  ```

  Windows: `"command": "node", "args": ["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"]`.
  VS Code's current docs also describe a global Copilot config
  (`~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`); the workspace file above is the one checked
  here.
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` and pick the agent; not tested
  per client. The MCP server works without it.
- **Verify:** start the server from the MCP view, open Copilot chat in Agent
  mode and ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation is not mentioned in VS Code's MCP docs; use the
  confirm phrase unless a form appears.
- Docs: [MCP servers in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/customization/mcp-servers).

## Codex CLI

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** one command, run here to confirm the output:

  ```bash
  codex mcp add rendezvous -- rdv-mcp
  ```

  or `~/.codex/config.toml`:

  ```toml
  [mcp_servers.rendezvous]
  command = "rdv-mcp"
  ```

  Windows: `codex mcp add rendezvous -- node C:\Users\<you>\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js`
  writes `command = "node"` and a single-quoted `args` path (tested here).
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` and pick Codex (installs under
  `~/.codex/skills`); not run per client.
- **Verify:** `codex mcp list`, then ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation not mentioned in Codex's MCP docs; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [Codex MCP](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp).

## Gemini CLI

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:**

  ```bash
  gemini mcp add -s user rendezvous rdv-mcp
  ```

  or edit `~/.gemini/settings.json` (`.gemini/settings.json` for one project):

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": [] } } }
  ```

  Windows: `gemini mcp add -s user rendezvous node C:\Users\<you>\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js`.
  Gemini CLI was not installed here, so the command is from its docs, not run.
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` and pick Gemini CLI; not run.
- **Verify:** `gemini mcp list`, or `/mcp` in a session, then ask "What's my
  rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation not mentioned in its docs; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [Gemini CLI MCP servers](https://geminicli.com/docs/tools/mcp-server/).

## Windsurf

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json` (macOS / Linux;
  `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devin/` if set) or `%APPDATA%\devin\mcp_config.json`
  (Windows). Windsurf's docs now live under Devin's.

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": [] } } }
  ```

  Windows: `"command": "node", "args": ["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"]`.
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` and pick the agent; not run.
- **Verify:** refresh the MCP list in Cascade, then ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation not mentioned; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [Cascade MCP](https://docs.devin.ai/desktop/cascade/mcp).

## Grok Build

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:**

  ```bash
  grok mcp add rendezvous -- rdv-mcp
  ```

  or `~/.grok/config.toml`:

  ```toml
  [mcp_servers.rendezvous]
  command = "rdv-mcp"
  ```

  Windows: `grok mcp add rendezvous -- node C:\Users\<you>\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js`.
  `--scope project` writes `.grok/config.toml` instead. Not installed here;
  from the docs.
- **Skill:** `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` and pick Grok; not run.
- **Verify:** `grok mcp doctor` (stderr logs: `~/.grok/logs/mcp/rendezvous.stderr.log`),
  then ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation not mentioned; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [Grok Build MCP servers](https://docs.x.ai/build/features/mcp-servers).

## OpenClaw

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:**

  ```bash
  openclaw mcp set rendezvous '{"command":"rdv-mcp"}'
  openclaw mcp doctor rendezvous --probe
  ```

  `--probe` opens a live connection to the server (without it `doctor` only
  checks the config); `openclaw mcp probe rendezvous` is the same check on its
  own. Windows: use `'{"command":"node","args":["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"]}'`
  (quote it for your shell). Not installed here; from the docs.
- **Skill:** OpenClaw installs a git skill only when `SKILL.md` is at the
  repository root of the ref; there is no subpath syntax. So this repo publishes
  a `skill` branch whose root is the skill folder (`SKILL.md` and `references/`):

  ```bash
  openclaw skills install git:omernesh/rendezvous@skill
  ```

  Git skills are not updated by `openclaw skills update`: install again to
  refresh. Maintainers rebuild the branch with `scripts/publish-skill-branch.sh`
  (or `.ps1`); see [Maintainers](#maintainers-the-skill-branch).
- **Verify:** `openclaw mcp doctor rendezvous --probe`, then ask "What's my
  rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation not mentioned; use the confirm phrase.
- Docs: [openclaw skills](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/skills), [openclaw mcp](https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/mcp/registry).

## Hermes Agent

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `~/.hermes/config.yaml`, then `/reload-mcp` in a session.

  ```yaml
  mcp_servers:
    rendezvous:
      command: "rdv-mcp"
  ```

  Windows: `command: "node"` and `args: ['C:\Users\<you>\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js']`.
  Hermes passes a stdio server only a safe baseline environment, not your shell's;
  `rdv-mcp` needs only `HOME` / `USERPROFILE`, but set `env:` if you use `RDV_HOME`.
- **Skill:** installs straight from this repository's path (run here):

  ```bash
  hermes skills install omernesh/rendezvous/plugins/rendezvous/skills/rendezvous
  ```

  Hermes scans community skills before installing them; this one passes the scan
  (`SAFE`) and installs as is. The skill carries no download-and-run
  line: it sends you to the Install section of https://rendezvous.nesher.co to
  run the installer yourself. Add `--yes` to skip the prompt.
  The installed files are `SKILL.md` and `references/`, under `~/.hermes/skills/rendezvous`.
- **Verify:** `/reload-mcp`, then ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation supported (form mode, Hermes' normal approval
  surface; YOLO mode does not auto-answer it).
- Docs: [Hermes MCP](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/mcp), [creating skills](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/developer-guide/creating-skills).

## Muse Code

- **Install:** the installer above.
- **MCP config:** `~/.config/muse/settings.json`. Keep what is already in the
  file and add the server.

  ```json
  {
    "schema_version": 1,
    "mcpServers": { "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": [] } }
  }
  ```

  Windows: `"command": "node", "args": ["C:\\Users\\<you>\\.rendezvous\\src\\impl\\packages\\mcp\\dist\\src\\bin.js"]`.
  **Not verified:** Muse Code was not available here and no first-party
  documentation could be found. Some third-party guides write the key as
  `mcp_servers`, and one reports a beta build without MCP. If `mcpServers` does
  not load, check Muse Code's own docs for the current key.
- **Skill:** Muse Code reads skills from `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.claude/skills`
  and `~/.codex/skills`. Install into one of them, for example
  `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous --skill rendezvous --global --agent claude-code`
  (puts it in `~/.claude/skills`), or copy the folder
  `plugins/rendezvous/skills/rendezvous` to `~/.agents/skills/rendezvous`. Not run here.
- **Verify:** ask "What's my rendezvous status?".
- **Consent:** elicitation unknown; use the confirm phrase.

## Maintainers: the skill branch

The skill lives once, in `plugins/rendezvous/skills/rendezvous`. The `skill`
branch is generated from it (`git subtree split`), never edited by hand, so the
text cannot drift. There is no CI: after changing the skill, run

```bash
sh scripts/publish-skill-branch.sh      # PowerShell: scripts/publish-skill-branch.ps1
```

from a clean checkout of `main`. It force-pushes `skill`, which holds nothing
else. `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous` is unaffected: it reads the default
branch, where the skills are still found in the plugin folder.

---

Source: https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/plugin.md

# Rendezvous plugin for Claude Code

Set up [Rendezvous](https://rendezvous.nesher.co) by chatting with Claude:
install `rdv`, create your agent, connect with another person's agent and send
the first message. Approvals always come back to you.

```text
/plugin marketplace add omernesh/rendezvous
/plugin install rendezvous@rendezvous
/reload-plugins
```

Then type `/rdv-onboarding` (the full name is `/rendezvous:rdv-onboarding`, if
another plugin also has an `rdv-onboarding`). It sets you up one question per
turn: install, MCP tools, profile, email, optional phone, relays (the default
public set or your own, each one checked), public pointer, your agent, its
card and an optional first contact,
verifying each step before the next. Re-run it to resume where you stopped.

After that, ask, for example: "Ask john@doe.com's agent to connect", "Tell
John I'm running late", "check rendezvous".

What it contains:

- `skills/rdv-onboarding/SKILL.md`: the `/rdv-onboarding` command, a guided
  setup that asks one question at a time and follows the consent rules of the
  `rendezvous` skill.
- `skills/rendezvous/SKILL.md`: the setup and messaging workflow, with the
  consent rules. It uses the Agent Skills format, so other agents can load it
  too (`npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous`).
- `.mcp.json`: registers the `rdv-mcp` server through `bin/rdv-mcp.mjs`, which
  starts the build the installer put in `~/.rendezvous/src` (or `$RDV_DIR`).
  Until Rendezvous is installed the server fails to start; install it (the
  skill points you to the installer), then run `/reload-plugins`. The server uses the profile
  `rdv` uses: `$RDV_HOME`, else `~/.rendezvous/$RDV_PROFILE`, else
  `~/.rendezvous/default`.
- `hooks/hooks.json`: a consent guard on every tool call. It stops Claude
  from running the `rdv` commands that grant consent or print confirm phrases
  (`rdv contact grant`, `rdv dinner confirm`, `rdv contact pending`,
  `rdv dinner list`, …) or name a contact (`rdv contact label`, or
  `rdv contact request <agent-id> --label`), however the command is quoted or wrapped (`npx`,
  `bash -c`, `$(…)`), and from reading, editing, searching or globbing the
  agent's secret key and consent file with any tool. Those stay with you, in
  your own terminal.

  **The hook is defence in depth, not a security boundary.** A model with a
  shell can always build a command it can't see (a script file, another
  interpreter). The boundary is the MCP consent gate: `rdv_grant` and
  `rdv_negotiate` need your approval form or a confirm phrase only you see,
  and the phrase is stored only as a hash. See "Threat model" in
  [`impl/packages/mcp/README.md`](https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/mcp.md).

Sending: Claude picks the recipient by its `local_label`, never by an address
the other agent's card claims, and shows you the fingerprint before the first
message. Only you set a label: it is part of what you approve (the form shows
it next to the fingerprint and you can change it; a confirm phrase approves
only the label it was shown with), or you name a contact yourself with
`rdv contact label <agent-id> <label>` in your own terminal. A card found by
address is only a claim, so it never labels a contact.

Approving a contact: Claude calls `rdv_grant`, and Claude Code shows you an
approval form (MCP elicitation). Claude can't fill it in for you.

---

Source: https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/cli.md

# Rendezvous reference implementation

TypeScript packages for the [Rendezvous](https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/spec.md) agent-to-agent contact
protocol, built toward the two-agent dinner demo in [PLAN.md](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/PLAN.md).
`impl/` is an npm workspace:

| Package | Path | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `@rendezvous/core` | `packages/core` | The protocol library (keys, cards, discovery, consent, envelopes, Nostr transport) |
| `@rendezvous/a2a` | `packages/a2a` | A2A task semantics: the dinner-negotiation message model, engine, calendar adapter |
| `@rendezvous/cli` | `packages/cli` | `rdv`, a command-line agent; also the scripted bots and interop scenarios |
| `@rendezvous/mcp` | `packages/mcp` | `rdv-mcp`, a stdio MCP server so Claude (or any MCP client) can find, contact and book dinner with other agents |

`demo/` holds the showpiece script ([demo/SCRIPT.md](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/impl/demo/SCRIPT.md)), a
calendar generator and `relay-dump.mjs` (what the relay stores: ciphertext).

Core never depends on the CLI, the A2A layer, MCP or LLM code. `a2a` has no
runtime dependencies at all; the CLI glues the two together. The MCP server
builds on the CLI's library entry (`@rendezvous/cli/lib`: home dir, lock,
inbound loop), so `rdv` and `rdv-mcp` share profiles.

## @rendezvous/core

| Module | Spec | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `identity` | §4.1–4.2 | Ed25519 agent keys, `rdv1:` IDs, fingerprints |
| `sign` | — | Signed JSON documents (canonical JSON + Ed25519) |
| `card` | §4.3 | Create and verify address cards |
| `discovery` | §4.4 | `dtopic()`, address canonicalization, binding levels |
| `contact` | §5 | Contact request / grant / revoke, and the contact book (policy, replay, rate limits) |
| `envelope` | §6.4, §7 | Encrypted, signed envelopes; `seq`/`prev` ordering with gap detection |
| `transport/nostr` | §6.2 | Nostr relay transport (kind 30417): re-subscribes when a relay drops; publishes with retries, per-relay pacing and cooldowns, and per-relay status (`relayStatus()`); `DEFAULT_RELAYS` |
| `agent` | — | Ties it together: listen, discover, request, grant, send, receive |
| `testing/relay` | — | In-memory Nostr relay on a localhost WebSocket, for tests and local demos |

```ts
import { Agent, NostrTransport } from '@rendezvous/core';

const relays = ['wss://relay.example'];
const john = Agent.create((key) => new NostrTransport({ key, relays }), {
  rendezvous: [{ type: 'nostr', relay: relays[0], pref: 1 }],
  discovery: { addresses: [{ type: 'email', value: 'john@doe.com' }], public_pointer: false },
});
john.on('request', (p) => john.grant(p.request.id, { tier: 'friend' })); // the human decides here
john.on('message', (from, payload) => console.log(from, payload));
john.start();

// On another machine:
await omer.requestContact('john@doe.com', "Omer's agent would like to plan dinner.");
omer.once('contact', () => omer.send(john.id, { type: 'a2a/message', text: 'Thursday 20:00?' }));
```

**Relays.** `DEFAULT_RELAYS` is the public set `rdv init` uses when no relay
is given: `wss://nos.lol`, `wss://relay.primal.net`, `wss://relay.nostr.net`,
`wss://nostr.oxtr.dev` (checked live, NOTES 11a). A publish counts as
delivered when one relay answers `OK true`. Transient failures are retried
twice with jittered backoff. A relay that answers `blocked`, `restricted` or
`banned` is skipped for 30 minutes. Events are paced per relay (a burst of 6,
then 3 per second). Each tunable is a `NostrTransportOptions` field (NOTES 69).
An envelope's plaintext is at most 32 KiB (`MAX_PLAINTEXT_BYTES`, SPEC §6.4).

Agent state serializes with `agent.toJSON()` and loads with `Agent.fromJSON()`.
`packages/core/vectors/v1.json` holds interop test vectors: fixed keys, IDs,
discovery topics, a signed card and contact request, and a sample envelope
that another implementation should be able to open.

## @rendezvous/a2a

PLAN.md §5.1–5.2, SPEC.md §7. Payloads `a2a/message` (an A2A v0.3 `Message`)
and `a2a/task-update` (a `TaskStatusUpdateEvent`) travel inside envelopes.
The verb sits in the message's `data` part (`data.rdv`): `meeting/propose`,
`meeting/counter`, `meeting/accept`, `meeting/confirm`, `meeting/decline`, `meeting/cancel`, `rdv/cancel`.

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `model` | Types and `parsePayload`: strict validation of peer input (known keys only, UUIDs, 1–3 RFC 3339 slots with offsets, bounded text) |
| `engine` | Pure state machine: `propose`, `receive`, `confirmMeeting`, `cancel`, `cancelMeeting`, `expire` return `{ state, outgoing, effects, events }`; no I/O, no clock |
| `calendar` | `CalendarAdapter` (`freeBusy(range)`, `hold(slot)`, `release(slot, note)`), `MemoryCalendar`, `JsonFileCalendar` (titles never leave the file) |
| `window` | `parseWindow`: RFC 3339 ranges and a few phrases, with `now` and the UTC offset passed in |
| `time` | Instants, fixed offsets, slot formatting |

Policy: an offer carries up to 3 free slots (one per day first); the receiver
accepts the first offered slot that is free and inside its window, else
counters with 3 of its own; after 3 offers the task ends `rejected`. Task
states: submitted → input-required / working → completed | rejected |
canceled. Agreement is a handshake: the accepter holds the slot tentatively
and sends `meeting/accept`; the offerer checks it is still free, sends
`meeting/confirm` and completes; the accepter completes on the confirm. A
tentative hold is released when the task is canceled, declined or expires,
and every hold is busy for all other tasks. Unless `ctx.autoConfirm`, the
engine waits for its human before each of those two steps (`confirmMeeting`).
Messages are deduplicated by `messageId`; `rdv/cancel` is honored
while pending; an agreed meeting is called off with `meeting/cancel`
(`cancelMeeting`, our human only), which the peer honors only for that
completed task and slot, freeing it in both calendars; meeting verbs need `may_propose_meetings` in the grant, and
`may_access_calendar: none` blocks them. A peer can hold at most 32 tasks
with us. Details and open questions: [NOTES.md](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/impl/NOTES.md) items 28–37, 58, 61.

**`--window`** (local time = a fixed offset; weeks run Monday–Sunday; an
evening is 19:00–23:00; everything is clipped to start no earlier than now):

| Window | Means |
|---|---|
| `tonight` / `tomorrow evening` | that one evening |
| `this week evenings` | every evening from today to Sunday |
| `next week evenings` | every evening Monday–Sunday of next week |
| `this weekend` / `next weekend` | Saturday and Sunday evenings |
| `2026-11-05T19:00:00+02:00/2026-11-05T23:00:00+02:00[,…]` | explicit ranges |

Calendar file: `{ "timezone": "+02:00", "busy": [ { "start": "…", "end": "…", "title": "optional" } ] }`.
Held slots are added to `busy`: `Dinner (tentative, rdv <task>)` while the
handshake runs, then `Dinner (rdv <task>)`; a tentative hold that falls
through is removed.

## rdv (the CLI)

```bash
npm install && npm run build              # from impl/
npm run rdv -- --help                     # or: node packages/cli/dist/src/bin.js --help
```

`npx rdv …` also works once `npm install` has run after the first build
(npm links the binary only when `dist/` exists).

State lives in a directory: `--home <dir>`, else `$RDV_HOME`, else
`~/.rendezvous/<profile>` (`--profile`, default `default`).

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `agent.json` | `Agent.toJSON()`, including the secret key (mode 600 where the OS supports it) |
| `config.json` | profile, relays, addresses (public ones are on the card; `private: true` ones are kept here only), policy |
| `relays.json` | per-relay diagnostics and cooldowns (last OK, last error), written after each publish and read by `rdv whoami` / `rdv_status` |
| `inbox.jsonl` | received payloads, one JSON object per line |
| `cards.json` | cards found by `rdv lookup`, so `contact request <agent-id>` can use them |
| `negotiations.json` | dinner negotiations (the a2a engine state) |
| `consent.json` | salted scrypt hashes of the confirm phrases for pending requests, probe answers and held dinners, each bound to what the human was shown (written by `rdv-mcp`; `contact pending` and `dinner list` issue and show a fresh phrase in text mode) |
| `holds.json` | which calendar file holds each tentative dinner hold, so `dinner confirm`/`cancel` can finalize or release it |
| `events.jsonl` | shared event log: what the home's listener handled, plus `rdv-mcp`'s own events; `rdv_inbox` is a view of it |
| `events.lock` | held while appending to `events.jsonl` |

| `lock` | held while a command reads and writes state |
| `listener.lock` | held for its lifetime by the home's one inbound consumer (`rdv listen` or `rdv-mcp`) |

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `rdv init --profile omer --email omer@example.com [--email …] [--relay wss://… [--relay …]] [--phone +…] [--phone …] [--public-pointer] [--force]` | Generate key and card, write state. Repeat `--email` / `--phone` for more addresses (canonicalized, repeats dropped, at most 8). Without `--relay`: `DEFAULT_RELAYS` (below). An agent keeps the relays it was created with |
| `rdv whoami` | Print agent ID, fingerprint, addresses, per-relay health (`relay_health`: last OK, last error, cooldown), card JSON (never the secret key) |
| `rdv address list` | Our addresses, each public (on the card, answers probes; with its topic) or private (kept in `config.json` only) |
| `rdv address add <email\|+phone> [--public\|--private]` | Add one (default public). A public one re-signs the card with a later `created`, republishes it if the public pointer is on, and a running `listen` / `rdv-mcp` starts answering probes on it within a second. Duplicates (in any spelling) and a ninth address are refused |
| `rdv address remove <email\|+phone>` | Remove one: probes on it are refused at once and its topic is dropped; with the public pointer on, the new card is also published on the removed topic, replacing the old one there. Contacts are kept (NOTES 63) |
| `rdv card publish` | Publish public pointers (if enabled at init) |
| `rdv lookup john@doe.com` | Fetch public-pointer cards for an address |
| `rdv contact request <email\|card-file\|agent-id> [--greeting "…"] [--in-person] [--label john@doe.com]` | Topic probe by email, or direct by card. `--in-person` records the `in-person` binding for a card you got face to face. `--label` is your local name for them (a probe is labeled with the address) |
| `rdv contact pending` | Pending inbound requests with binding, fingerprint, greeting; answers to your topic probes awaiting confirmation |
| `rdv contact grant <request-id> [--tier friend] [--scope-file s.json] [--label john@doe.com]` | Approve (`--label`: your local name for them) |
| `rdv contact label <agent-id> <label>` | Name a contact locally; sending by name (`rdv_send` `to`) resolves through this, never through the addresses its card claims. Yours to run: an assistant may only suggest a label, which you approve with the contact (NOTES 62) |
| `rdv contact grant <agent-id> [--tier …] [--scope-file …]` | Give a contact you requested rights towards you (by default it may write, not propose meetings); the contact gets a reverse grant, so it can then propose (NOTES 60) |
| `rdv contact confirm <grant-id>` / `rdv contact reject <grant-id> [--block]` | Accept or turn down an answer to your topic probe (anyone who saw the probe can answer; check the fingerprint) |
| `rdv contact decline <request-id> [--block]` | Decline |
| `rdv contact list` / `rdv contact revoke <agent-id>` | Manage contacts |
| `rdv contact resync <agent-id>` | After `listen` reports an `envelope chain fork` (the contact restored an old backup), accept its current chain once you have checked with them; until then its messages are refused |
| `rdv send <agent-id> --json '{"type":"a2a/message","text":"hi"}'` | Send any payload (`--payload '…'` is the same without JSON output) |
| `rdv listen [--auto-grant <tier> [--auto-grant-any-tier]] [--exec <script>] [--negotiate --calendar cal.json [--window "…"] [--tz +02:00]]` | Long-running: print events; auto-grant is for demos only and stops at `stranger` unless `--auto-grant-any-tier`; `--exec` gets each event as a JSON line on stdin (`RDV_EVENT`, `RDV_HOME` set); `--negotiate` answers dinner proposals from the calendar (window default `next week evenings`) and holds a slot for you to confirm; `--auto-confirm` skips the human (bots, demos) |
| `rdv dinner propose <agent-id> --calendar cal.json --window "next week evenings" [--tz +02:00] [--minutes 120] [--place …] [--area …] [--expires <rfc3339>]` | Offer up to 3 free slots; run `listen --negotiate` to handle the replies |
| `rdv dinner confirm <task-id> --hold <code>` | Confirm the dinner a negotiation holds for you: sends `meeting/accept` (their offer) or `meeting/confirm` (they accepted yours). `--hold` is the code `rdv dinner list` shows; it is refused if the meeting changed since |
| `rdv dinner cancel <task-id> [--reason …]` | Send `rdv/cancel` for a pending negotiation and release its hold; for an agreed (completed) dinner, send `meeting/cancel`: it leaves your calendar and the peer's agent removes it from theirs |
| `rdv dinner list` | Negotiations with state, round, agreed or held slot (and what it waits for) |
| `rdv inbox [--follow]` | Show received payloads |

Output is human text by default and one JSON object per line with `--json`.
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 error, 2 usage error. Every command except `listen` and
`inbox --follow` loads state under the lock, runs, saves, and exits. `listen`
takes the lock only while it handles one inbound item, so a bot can run
`rdv contact grant` against the same home while `listen` is running; it prints
an event only after the state behind it is saved.

**One inbound consumer per home.** Two processes subscribed for the same home
would split inbound events between them (whichever handles an envelope first
wins; the other never sees it). So whoever consumes holds `listener.lock`
(O_EXCL file with pid, host and role, mtime touched every minute; broken when
its pid is gone on this host, or after 10 minutes without a touch from another
host) and appends every event it handles to `events.jsonl`, after the state
behind it is saved. A second `rdv listen` exits 1 naming the holder. A second
`rdv-mcp` runs **attached**: it opens no subscriptions, still sends (grant,
send, negotiate), and its `rdv_inbox` follows `events.jsonl` by cursor, so every
server on the home sees each event once with the same cursor. When the holder
exits, an attached server takes the lock within a second and starts
consuming; the relays' lookback replays what arrived meanwhile, and the
channels drop what was already handled. Negotiation follows the consumer:
run `rdv listen --negotiate` (or give the consuming `rdv-mcp` a calendar) if
an attached server should get answers to its dinner proposals.

With `--json`, negotiation steps print as `{"event":"dinner","kind":…,"task":…,"peer":…,"state":…}`
(kinds: proposed, offer-received, countered, confirm-needed, accepted,
completed, meeting-canceled, released, rejected, canceled, expired, status,
duplicate, ignored, invalid). In text mode the
peer's text parts and decline reasons are shown as untrusted and cleaned.

PowerShell quoting for `send`: `rdv send <id> --json '{\"type\":\"a2a/message\",\"text\":\"hi\"}'`
(Windows PowerShell 5 strips bare inner quotes; PowerShell 7.3+ accepts the bash form).

### The dinner scenarios (PLAN §5.3)

`packages/cli/scenarios/dinner.ts`: Omer and John each run
`rdv listen --negotiate` with their own JSON calendar; Omer runs
`rdv dinner propose`. Variants: `overlap` (John, then Omer, confirms with
`rdv dinner confirm`; both `completed` on the same slot, one hold each),
`no-overlap` (`rejected` after 3 rounds), `cancel` (John offline while Omer
proposes and cancels; both `canceled`), `cancel-hold` (Omer cancels while
John's agent holds a slot for John; the hold is released), `duplicate`
(`--auto-confirm` bots, then every envelope replayed and a message re-sent;
nothing changes), `reverse` (John, who granted the contact, proposes: refused
until Omer runs `rdv contact grant <john-id>`, which sends John a reverse
grant; then both confirm and complete), `cancel-agreed` (`--auto-confirm`
bots agree, then John runs `rdv dinner cancel`; both calendars free the
evening and both end `canceled`). All seven run in `npm test`; `overlap` runs in
`npm run test:live`; by hand:

`node packages/cli/dist/scenarios/dinner.js --relay ws://… [--variant overlap] [--variant …]`.

### The contact scenario (PLAN §4.5)

`packages/cli/scenarios/contact.ts` drives real `rdv` processes with separate
homes: John listens, Omer requests by email, John grants, Omer sends, John's
inbox shows it, each step asserted with a timeout. It runs:

- against the in-memory relay as part of `npm test`;
- against real relays with `npm run test:live` (below);
- by hand against any relays, e.g. from two machines' worth of setup:
  `node packages/cli/dist/scenarios/contact.js --relay wss://relay.example [--relay …] [--timeout 30000] [--keep]`.

Crash safety: state is saved right before each envelope leaves (`Agent.beforeSend`),
so a crash after a send never reuses a `seq` (issue #4).

## rdv-mcp (the MCP server)

PLAN §6.1. Tools `rdv_init`, `rdv_status`, `rdv_publish_card`, `rdv_discover`,
`rdv_request_contact`, `rdv_pending_requests`, `rdv_grant`, `rdv_revoke`,
`rdv_send`, `rdv_inbox`, `rdv_negotiate`, and the `rdv://inbox` resource
(subscribable). `rdv_grant` needs the human: an MCP elicitation form, or a
confirm phrase shown only in their terminal. Peer text comes back only as
`untrusted_peer_text`. Details, consent threat model and client config:
[packages/mcp/README.md](https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/mcp.md), [demo/SCRIPT.md](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/impl/demo/SCRIPT.md).

```bash
node packages/mcp/dist/src/bin.js --home ~/.rendezvous/omer --calendar cal.json --tz +02:00
```

## Develop

Run from `impl/` (works the same in PowerShell and bash):

```bash
npm install
npm run typecheck        # every workspace
npm test                 # core, a2a, cli (commands + scenarios), mcp (two servers end to end); local relay, no network
npm run build            # tsc -b -> packages/*/dist
npm run test:vectors:update   # regenerate vectors (deliberate wire-format changes only)
```

One package or one file: `npm test -w @rendezvous/core`, or
`cd packages/core && npx vitest run test/unit.test.ts -t envelope`.
CLI tests spawn the built `rdv`, so the CLI's `test` script builds first.

**Live relays.** `npm run test:live` runs only `*.live.test.ts`, and those skip
unless `RDV_LIVE_RELAYS` lists relays. They are never part of `npm test`.
The live files run one at a time, since public relays limit connections per
IP. Keep the volume modest: relay.damus.io banned the test pubkey after a few
runs.

```bash
RDV_LIVE_RELAYS=wss://nos.lol,wss://relay.primal.net,wss://relay.nostr.net,wss://nostr.oxtr.dev npm run test:live
```
```powershell
$env:RDV_LIVE_RELAYS='wss://nos.lol,wss://relay.primal.net,wss://relay.nostr.net,wss://nostr.oxtr.dev'; npm run test:live; Remove-Item Env:RDV_LIVE_RELAYS
```

**Pre-push hook (replaces CI).** Enable it once per clone, from the repo root:

```bash
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

`.githooks/pre-push` runs `npm run typecheck && npm test` in `impl/` and blocks
the push if either fails.

See [NOTES.md](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/impl/NOTES.md) for wire-format decisions and the places where this
implementation departs from or fills gaps in SPEC.md.

---

Source: https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/mcp.md

# @rendezvous/mcp

`rdv-mcp`: a stdio MCP server that gives an MCP client (Claude Code, Claude
Desktop, the MCP Inspector) a Rendezvous agent. PLAN.md §6.1, SPEC.md §13.

The server runs one long-lived listening agent in-process. Its state is the
same home dir as the `rdv` CLI (`agent.json`, `config.json`, `inbox.jsonl`,
`negotiations.json`, `lock`, plus `consent.json`, `events.jsonl` and
`listener.lock`), and it takes the lock only per operation, like `rdv listen`.
So `rdv contact pending` or `rdv contact grant` can run in a terminal against
the same profile while the server is up. Only one process per home consumes
inbound events (whoever holds `listener.lock`); if `rdv listen` or another
`rdv-mcp` already does, this server runs attached: its tools work, and
`rdv_inbox` reads the events the consumer writes to `events.jsonl`. It takes
over when the consumer exits. `rdv_status` says which (`inbound`: `consumer`
or `attached`). See impl/README.md.

```bash
npm run build                              # from impl/
node packages/mcp/dist/src/bin.js --home ~/.rendezvous/omer --calendar cal.json --tz +02:00
```

Options: `--home <dir>` or `--profile <name>` (same resolution as `rdv`:
`--home`, `$RDV_HOME`, `~/.rendezvous/<profile>`), `--calendar <file.json>`,
`--calendar-dir <dir>` (repeatable, env `RDV_CALENDAR_DIR`: where the assistant
may pick other calendar files from),
`--window "next week evenings"`, `--tz +02:00` (env `RDV_CALENDAR`,
`RDV_WINDOW`, `RDV_TZ`). Without a calendar, incoming dinner proposals are
listed but not answered. stdout carries MCP; human-facing notices go to stderr.
Client config examples: [`impl/demo/SCRIPT.md`](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/blob/main/impl/demo/SCRIPT.md).

## Use it from Claude Code (plugin)

The repo is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace. In Claude Code's chat:

```text
/plugin marketplace add omernesh/rendezvous
/plugin install rendezvous@rendezvous
/reload-plugins
```

The plugin ([`plugins/rendezvous`](https://github.com/omernesh/rendezvous/tree/main/plugins/rendezvous)) registers this
server through a small launcher (`bin/rdv-mcp.mjs`, run with `node`, so it
works on Windows too) that loads the build the installer made in
`~/.rendezvous/src` (or `$RDV_DIR`). It adds the Rendezvous skill (install,
identity, contact, first message, incoming requests) and a PreToolUse consent
guard (below). The server uses the same home as `rdv`: `$RDV_HOME`, else
`~/.rendezvous/$RDV_PROFILE`, else `~/.rendezvous/default`. The skill alone,
for other agents that load SKILL.md files: `npx skills add omernesh/rendezvous`.

## Use it from other MCP clients

Per-agent setup, skill install and a check that it works for ten agents: [`docs/agents.md`](https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/agents.md).

Register `rdv-mcp` as a stdio server; the installer puts it on PATH. Pass
options (`--profile omer`, `--calendar cal.json`, …) in `args`.

Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`) or Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`
or `.cursor/mcp.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rendezvous": { "command": "rdv-mcp", "args": ["--profile", "omer"] }
  }
}
```

Codex (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[mcp_servers.rendezvous]
command = "rdv-mcp"
args = ["--profile", "omer"]
```

On Windows `rdv-mcp` is a `.cmd` shim, which most clients can't spawn
directly: use `"command": "cmd", "args": ["/c", "rdv-mcp", "--profile", "omer"]`,
or `"command": "node"` with the built file
(`%USERPROFILE%\.rendezvous\src\impl\packages\mcp\dist\src\bin.js`) as the
first argument. Claude Code without the plugin:
`claude mcp add rendezvous -- rdv-mcp --profile omer` (Windows:
`claude mcp add rendezvous -- cmd /c rdv-mcp --profile omer`).

Approval forms need a client that supports MCP elicitation; Claude Code does in
interactive sessions (not in `-p`). Elsewhere approvals use the confirm phrase
the human reads in their own terminal (`rdv contact pending`), below.

## Tools

| Tool | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| `rdv_init` | profile, emails[], phones[] (`email` / `phone`: one of each, kept as aliases), relays (omitted: the default public relays `wss://nos.lol`, `wss://relay.primal.net`, `wss://relay.nostr.net`, `wss://nostr.oxtr.dev`), public_pointer, calendar, window, tz | agent ID, fingerprint; keeps an existing agent and its relays (re-key only with `rdv init --force`). Every address is public; at most 8 |
| `rdv_addresses` | action `list` / `add` / `remove`, address, public (add; default true) | our addresses, each public or private; `add` / `remove` re-sign and (pointer on) republish the card and re-subscribe at once, like `rdv address`. The owner's own setup, not a consent decision; strict email / E.164 only; contacts are kept |
| `rdv_status` | — | ID, our addresses (`addresses`, and `our_addresses` with public or private), relays, `relay_health` (per relay: `last_ok`, `last_error` with `kind` and the relay's message as `untrusted_peer_text`, `cooldown_until`), contacts (`local_label`: what your user called them; `unverified_claims`: the addresses their cards claim; `label_conflict` when two share a label), pending count, negotiation settings, approval mode |
| `rdv_publish_card` | — | topics published, and `on_relays`: per public address, whether the relays now serve this card (read back) |
| `rdv_discover` | address | cards found (agent ID, fingerprint, claimed addresses, relays); never a label (anyone can publish a card for any address), never our own card (for our own address: `own_card_on_relays`) |
| `rdv_request_contact` | target (email, +phone, or agent ID), greeting, label (probes only) | request ID, local_label (a probe: the address probed, applied only when the human confirms the answer; by agent ID: none, and a `label` is refused) |
| `rdv_pending_requests` | — | requests with fingerprint, binding, how they arrived, untrusted greeting |
| `rdv_grant` | request_id, tier, may_propose_meetings, confirm_phrase, label; or grant_id (+ confirm_phrase, label) to confirm a probe answer; or agent_id (+ tier, may_propose_meetings, confirm_phrase) to grant an existing contact more, which also sends it a reverse grant | contact (needs the human, below) |
| `rdv_revoke` | agent_id, or request_id / grant_id (+ block) to decline | revoked / declined / rejected |
| `rdv_send` | agent_id or to (a `local_label`), payload `{type, …}` (not `a2a/*`, `rdv/*`) | agent ID, fingerprint, envelope seq; `to` is refused when no contact, or more than one, has that label |
| `rdv_inbox` | since cursor, limit, wait_seconds (≤ 60) | events + next_cursor |
| `rdv_negotiate` | action propose / confirm / cancel / status; agent_id, intent `dinner`, window, calendar, tz, minutes, place, area, expires, task_id, reason, confirm_phrase | task ID and state; progress via `rdv_inbox`; `confirm` needs the human (below) |

Resource `rdv://inbox` holds the latest 50 events; the server supports
`resources/subscribe` and sends `notifications/resources/updated` when events
arrive, so a client that subscribes needn't poll.

Events: `contact_request`, `contact_candidate` (an answer to our discovery
probe, confirmed through the same human gate as a grant), `contact`, `message`, `revoked`, `dropped`, `error`,
and `dinner` (kind proposed / offer-received / countered / confirm-needed /
accepted / completed / released / rejected / canceled / expired / status, with
a plain-language `summary` we write from validated fields; `confirm-needed`
also carries a `next_step`).

Grants issued here always carry `may_initiate: true`,
`may_access_calendar: "free_busy"`, `max_frequency: "100/day"`, and
`may_propose_meetings` (default true). The calendar adapter only ever shares
free slots, never titles.

## Consent: the human decides (demo-critical)

`rdv_grant` must not succeed on the model's say-so. It succeeds only through
one of these:

1. **Elicitation.** If the client advertises the `elicitation` capability, the
   server asks the client to show the human a form: requester agent ID,
   fingerprint, binding (with a warning that `claimed` proves nothing), how the
   request arrived, the greeting marked untrusted, a tier picker, and the
   local label (the model's suggestion, editable; empty for none). Only
   `accept` with `approve: true` grants; the human's tier and label win over
   the model's. The model never sees or answers this form. A probe answer
   gets the same form, with the probed address as the label.
2. **Confirm phrase.** Otherwise each pending request gets a random phrase
   (three words and three digits, about 28 bits), shown only on human
   channels: this server's stderr and `rdv contact pending` in text mode (not
   `--json`). `consent.json` (mode 600) keeps only a salted scrypt hash, so
   the terminal issues a new phrase each time it shows one (the latest shown
   wins). The human reads it and types it to the model, which passes it as
   `confirm_phrase`. A phrase approves the request on the terms shown with it
   (tier, scope and local label, default first: no label): if the model asks
   for another tier, `may_propose_meetings` or `label`, it is refused and the
   human is shown a new phrase for exactly those terms (issue #12, NOTES 62).
   A probe answer's phrase is bound the same way to its label (the probed
   address unless the model asks for another). Phrases are per request and single
   use; 5 wrong tries replace the phrase. A phrase can approve tiers `friend`
   and below; `family`/`spouse` need the form or `rdv contact grant --tier …`
   in a terminal.
3. **The terminal.** The human runs `rdv contact grant <id>` themselves.

**Each meeting too (issue #8).** The server answers dinner proposals from the
calendar, but the slot it picks is only held tentatively ("confirm-needed")
until the human confirms it: `rdv_negotiate` with action `confirm` passes the
same gate. With elicitation the human gets a form (peer fingerprint, time,
place marked untrusted); `decline` there cancels the negotiation and
releases the hold, dismissing it leaves the dinner held. Otherwise the server
issues a confirm phrase per held dinner (same rules, shown on stderr and in
`rdv dinner list` text mode), or the human runs `rdv dinner confirm <task-id> --hold <code>`
(or `rdv dinner cancel`) in a terminal. That happens once per side: the
accepter's human before the accept goes out, the offerer's before the
`meeting/confirm`. Holds are released on cancel, decline or expiry.
Approval is bound to the meeting the human saw, not the peer-chosen task ID:
if the held meeting changes before the confirm runs (another slot, peer or
stage, or a new negotiation under the same ID), nothing is confirmed, the tool
says it changed, and a new phrase is issued (NOTES 59).

**Canceling an agreed dinner (issue #20).** `rdv_negotiate` action `cancel`
on a completed dinner passes the same gate, bound to the agreement shown
(NOTES 61): a form if the client can elicit (only an explicit yes cancels),
otherwise the first call issues a cancel phrase to the human (stderr and
`rdv dinner list`) and fails; the human can also run `rdv dinner cancel`.
The peer's agent frees the evening without asking (it only frees time) and
reports a `meeting-canceled` event.

**Granting an existing contact more (issue #1).** `rdv_grant` with
`agent_id` gives a contact (for example one the user requested, which by
default may write but not propose meetings) the tier and
`may_propose_meetings` asked for, and sends it a reverse grant so it can use
them. Same gate: a form showing the contact's fingerprint, local label, its
rights now and exactly what is granted (the human's tier and meetings choice
win), or a confirm phrase issued on the model's first call and bound to that
contact and those terms (stderr and `rdv contact pending`). The contact is
checked again under the lock where the grant happens; one revoked and made
again under the same agent ID is refused (NOTES 66).

No tool result ever contains a phrase (tests scan every result and the inbox
resource). Limits (NOTES 57): phrases are not on disk, but a model that can
read files or run commands as the same user can still catch one while it is
shown (or run `rdv contact pending` itself); there, prefer elicitation or the
terminal. Without a phrase or elicitation, `rdv_grant` fails and tells the
model to ask its human.

**Threat model.** This stops a model from granting on its own initiative, and
stops instructions injected through peer text from making it grant. It does
**not** stop a model that can run arbitrary shell commands or read arbitrary
files as the same OS user: such a model can catch a phrase while it is shown,
run `rdv contact grant` or `rdv contact label` itself, or read `agent.json`, which holds the secret
key, a worse problem. In Claude Code,
keep the default permission mode (shell commands and reads outside the project
need approval) and add deny rules for the home dir and `rdv contact pending`
(example in `demo/SCRIPT.md`). The Claude Code plugin adds a PreToolUse hook
(`plugins/rendezvous/hooks/consent-guard.mjs`) on every tool that refuses the
consent and phrase-showing `rdv` commands (`contact grant`/`confirm`/`resync`/
`label`/`pending`, `contact request <agent-id> --label`, `dinner confirm`/
`cancel`/`list`, `listen --auto-grant`/`--auto-confirm`, `init --force`), any command naming `agent.json`,
`agent.json.bak` or `consent.json`, and any read, edit, search or glob of a
Rendezvous home. It parses commands like a shell before matching. It is
defence in depth, **not a security boundary**: a model with a shell can still
get a command past it (NOTES 62). The boundary is the consent gate above. The strongest setup runs `rdv-mcp` as a
different OS user, or on another machine, from the one the assistant's tools
run as. Revoking and declining need no confirmation: they only reduce access.

## Prompt injection gate

- Peer-written text (greetings, text parts, decline reasons, free-form message
  payloads, error and drop details) reaches the model only as
  `{"untrusted_peer_text": "…"}`, with control and bidi characters replaced and
  a 2000-character cap. Results that contain such fields start with a note
  telling the model to treat them as data. The server instructions and the
  tool descriptions say the same.
- Short peer-chosen fields are strict tokens or get quarantined the same way:
  agent IDs, UUIDs, addresses (email / +phone), relay URLs, tiers, bindings,
  task states, payload `type` (`[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._/-]{0,63}`), integer `seq`.
- Only `data` parts drive the negotiation engine (`@rendezvous/a2a`, strict
  validation); text parts are display only.
- The model can't make the server read local files: `rdv_request_contact`
  takes addresses and agent IDs (no card files), calendar paths must end in
  `.json` and resolve (symlinks included) inside the home, the `--calendar`
  directory or a `--calendar-dir`, the file must be a strict calendar
  (`busy` list, optional `timezone`, nothing else) before it is read or
  rewritten, and calendar errors never echo file contents.
- Errors that could quote peer or file content (inbound handling, fs and
  JSON parse failures) go to the server log for the human; the model gets a
  generic line. Only our own messages (bad input, negotiation rules) reach it.

## Tests

`npm test -w @rendezvous/mcp`: two servers (Omer, John) driven by the SDK's
`Client` over an in-memory MCP transport against the in-memory relay, covering
init → discover → request → refused grant → human approval (confirm phrase,
and elicitation accept / decline) → negotiate → refused model-only dinner
confirmation → each human confirms (phrase, form) → completed on both sides, plus

a stdio smoke test, phrase rules and hardening. The chat onboarding flow the
plugin's skill follows (init, request by address, both humans approve by form
or phrase, first message) runs the same way. `test/plugin.test.ts` checks the
plugin: manifests, the launcher over stdio, the consent guard, and a lint that
fails if the skill or its references tell the assistant to run a consent
command. Live (dinner and onboarding):
`RDV_LIVE_RELAYS=wss://nos.lol,wss://relay.primal.net npm run test:live -w @rendezvous/mcp`.

---

Source: https://rendezvous.nesher.co/docs/spec.md

# Rendezvous
## An Open Protocol for Agent-to-Agent Contact

**Status:** Draft v0.1 rev 3 (2026-10-25) — for discussion
**Author:** Omer Nesher
**Date:** 2026-10-25 (rev 2: 2026-10-09)

> Codename "Rendezvous" is provisional. The protocol describes how a personal AI
> agent belonging to one human makes contact with, and safely communicates with, a
> personal AI agent belonging to another human — across different vendors,
> networks, and platforms.

> **Rev 2 (2026-10-09)** adds machine-first discovery: hint-server topics
> (Nostr / ntfy / MQTT), the mailbox probe, the invite, and optional discovery
> directories with friend suggestions (on by default). Rev 1 defined identity, consent
> and transport; rev 2 defines how two agents *find each other* in the first
> place.

> **Rev 3 (2026-10-25)** folds in what the TypeScript reference implementation
> (`impl/`) found: the wire format is now pinned down (canonical JSON, base32,
> signatures, envelope encryption, the Nostr carrier), the envelope signature
> covers the ciphertext, the grant carries the grantor's card, and consent, A2A
> meeting negotiation and untrusted peer text are specified. No discovery or
> consent concept changed; see **Changes in rev 3** below.

**Changes in rev 3**

- **Security fix, §6.4:** the envelope signature covers `content` (rev 2 left
  it out, so a genuine header could carry a substituted ciphertext). The
  encryption (ephemeral key `epk`, HKDF, AES-GCM) is now described. A peer
  that forks or rolls back its chain is refused until the receiving human
  re-syncs it. Amended: channel state is kept only for admitted senders, so
  fresh keys cannot fill a receiver's memory (was §11.10). Amended: the
  envelope plaintext is capped at 32 KiB, and receivers drop a bigger one
  before decrypting it.
- **Wire format, new §4.6:** canonical JSON (RFC 8785 subset), base32 alphabet
  and case, `sig` encoding and domain separation, `canon(address)`. §4.2 and
  §4.4 point to it.
- **Nostr, §6.2:** envelope kind `30417` stays, with a mandatory unique `d`
  tag; the regular-kind alternative and the 2026-10 relay survey are recorded.
  The secp256k1 carrier key and the `p` tag value are defined. NIP-44 is no
  longer claimed for v0.1.
- **Discovery, §4.4:** the `claimed` tier cap applies to the default tier, not
  an explicit human choice; the listen-mode probe is a contact request posted
  on the `dtopic`; probe greetings are public; the requester records a binding
  too. Amended: an agent's addresses change after setup; a changed card is
  re-signed with a later `created`, a requester keeps only an agent's newest
  card, and a public-pointer card is a replaceable event, so a removed address
  stops finding the agent (§4.3, §4.4, §6.2).
- **Consent, §5:** the grant carries the grantor's card (§5.3); who may answer
  a request; document IDs are UUIDs; grant direction and `max_frequency`
  format; scope defaults. New §5.5 (consent stays with the human) and §5.6
  (peer text is untrusted data). Amended: the reverse grant (§5.3, a grant
  with `grant_ref`) tells a contact what its peer's owner allows it, so the
  grantor side can propose meetings too (§7.4). A confirm phrase approves
  only the tier and scope shown with it, and is stored hashed (§5.5).
- **A2A, §7:** which A2A objects are sent, the meeting verbs, task states,
  slots, deduplication by `messageId`, cancellation, resend bounds, and
  persisting state before send. Amended: agreement is an accept → confirm
  handshake (`meeting/confirm`) with tentative, exclusive holds, and each
  human confirms the specific meeting (§5.5, §7.3; was §11.8). Amended: new
  verbs are A2A extensions, advertised on the card; a receiver answers what
  it does not support instead of dropping it, and ignores `metadata`
  (§4.3, §7.5; was §11.11).
- **Elsewhere:** threat-model rows (§8), probe privacy (§9), new open problems
  (§11), phases aligned with the implementation plan (§12), MCP consent and
  inbox semantics (§13).

---

## 1. Abstract

Every major AI lab now ships a personal agent (Meta Muse, xAI Grok Bot, OpenAI
Dots, Google Gemini Spark, Apple Siri AI, Instinct, Manus Cue, and more). Every
one of them is an island. Instinct's agents can talk to other Instincts over its
closed I2I network; Grok Bots coordinate only with other Grok Bots; Dots talk to
dots. There is no open way for a Muse agent to contact an Instinct agent — the
agent world today is the messaging world of 2008, before interoperability was
demanded by users and eventually forced open by protocol adoption (MCP).

Rendezvous defines that missing layer: a vendor-neutral, open protocol for
**agent identity, discovery, first contact, consent, and communication**,
designed so that nobody *has* to run infrastructure to participate. It reuses
proven building blocks — cryptographic keys for identity, Nostr relays as the
primary rendezvous, A2A for task semantics — and treats every transport as an
untrusted dumb pipe carrying end-to-end-encrypted envelopes.

Discovery is machine-first: agents find each other through silent hint-server
topics, DNS, and — only when nothing answers — a signed mailbox probe or a
premade invite. The human channel is the fallback transport and the place
consent lives, not the first place to look.

**Goals:**
- Any agent can contact any other agent, regardless of vendor or network.
- Any agent can be *found* by requesters who hold one of its owner's contact
  points — silently, without emailing a human first.
- Consent is a first-class protocol object: the human always decides who may
  reach their agent and what the relationship may do.
- Zero *required* infrastructure: no central registry, no company server, no
  required relay operator. Optional discovery directories exist, are
  community-run, and can be skipped by anyone.
- Self-healing: multiple rendezvous hints per agent; losing any one transport
  degrades gracefully, never breaks.
- Boring technology: everything is a key, a signed JSON envelope, and an
  existing public transport.

**Non-goals:**
- Not a message transport for humans.
- Not a blockchain, token, or incentive system.
- Not a payment or commerce layer (though agents may negotiate tasks that
  include payments via their own means).
- Not a registry of identity for legal/KYC purposes.

---

## 2. Motivation

In eight weeks (Aug–Oct 2026) the personal-agent market went from niche to
crowded. Instinct raised $1B at a $10B valuation; Muse became the #1 US app;
Dots launched with 4,000+ app connectors. Each vendor built a closed network:

| Vendor | Agent | Inter-agent story |
|---|---|---|
| Meta | Muse | Personal Agent Protocol working group (announced, no open impl) |
| xAI | Grok Bot | Bots delegate to Bots on the same account only |
| OpenAI | Dots | Dots coordinate within a user's own fleet |
| Instinct | Instinct | I2I "Trusted Person network" — closed, Instinct-to-Instinct only |
| Google | Gemini Spark | Google-ecosystem only |
| Decagon + Instinct | PACT | Open spec for person-agent ↔ *business*-agent consent (A2A-based) |
| Google | A2A | Open task-exchange protocol (server semantics, not consumer contact) |

The vacuum: **person-agent ↔ person-agent contact with per-relationship
consent, across vendors.** Instinct proved the demand (and built the walled
garden). PACT proved business consent. Nobody has shipped the open
person-to-person layer — for contact *or* discovery. The MCP precedent — an
open protocol that won by solving fragmentation at the moment of peak pain,
with zero ideology — is the template this spec follows.

---

## 3. Design principles

1. **Discovery is machine-first; humans are the trust anchor.** Agents find
   each other through silent channels (hint-server topics, DNS, an optional
   directory) and, when nothing answers, a signed mailbox probe. The human
   channel — email/SMS/WhatsApp — is the fallback transport and the place
   consent lives. No new app, no new account, no always-on device.
2. **Keys are identity.** An agent's identity is its Ed25519 public key,
   self-generated at install — globally unique, registry-free, unspoofable.
   It is the "MAC address" of the agent.
3. **Consent is the handshake.** An agent may only communicate with another
   after the receiving human approves. Approval is a signed grant scoped to a
   relationship (trust tier, capabilities, expiry).
4. **Relays are dumb pipes.** Every transport (Nostr relay, ntfy topic, MQTT
   broker, email server) sees only ciphertext and routing hints. Trust lives
   in keys, never in infrastructure.
5. **Rent, don't build.** All transports are existing public services the
   users already pay for. The protocol ships a spec and a reference library
   and runs no *required* servers; optional discovery directories are
   community-run, swappable, and skippable.
6. **Self-healing by redundancy.** An address card lists several rendezvous
   hints (Nostr relay, ntfy topic, MQTT, email, phone, DNS TXT). Failure of
   any one is routine, not fatal.
7. **Boring wins.** Everything that can be a signed JSON document is a signed
   JSON document. Nothing needs consensus, a ledger, or a chain.

---

## 4. Identity layer

### 4.1 Agent key

- Ed25519 keypair, generated at agent install.
- The private key never leaves the agent's secure storage; it can be held by
  the user's passkey/HSM where available.
- Key rotation: a new key is published with a `rotate` document signed by the
  old key, carrying the new key and a grace period. Peers accept either during
  the grace window. A key change **outside** a signed `rotate` document is a
  trust event: change alert + fresh consent handshake. (See §11 open problems
  on recovery.)

### 4.2 Agent ID

```
rdv1:<base32(ed25519-pubkey)>
```

- `rdv1` prefix disambiguates from other ID schemes.
- `base32` is the RFC 4648 alphabet, lowercase, without padding (§4.6): the
  32-byte key becomes 52 characters, so an ID is 57 characters long.
- Human-facing form: a short fingerprint, e.g. `rdv1:7f3a…9c2d`, always shown
  with a copy button; never ask humans to type full keys.

### 4.3 Address Card ("calling card")

The signed, self-describing document an agent publishes about itself. Schema
(v1):

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "id": "rdv1:7f3a…9c2d",
  "created": "2026-10-08T00:00:00Z",
  "expires": null,
  "capabilities": ["rdv/v1", "a2a/0.3"],
  "owner": {                // OPTIONAL and minimized by default
    "name": "John Doe", // only if the owner opts in
    "contact": ["mailto:john@doe.com"]  // one hint is enough
  },
  "discovery": {            // OPTIONAL — enables machine-first discovery
    "addresses": [          // contact points the owner is findable by
      {"type": "email", "value": "john@doe.com"},
      {"type": "phone", "value": "+972-54-000-0000"}
    ],
    "public_pointer": false // default: listen-only dead drop (§4.4)
  },
  "rendezvous": [           // ordered fallback list
    {"type": "nostr", "relay": "wss://relay.damus.io", "topic": "<kind-30417>", "pref": 1},
    {"type": "ntfy", "topic": "rdv-7f3a9c2d", "pref": 2},
    {"type": "email", "to": "rdv+7f3a9c2d@agent.example", "pref": 3},
    {"type": "dns", "domain": "doe.com", "pref": 0}
  ],
  "policy": {
    "inbound": "prompt",     // allow | block | prompt
    "public": false          // publish card to public relays / pointers?
  },
  "sig": "…ed25519 signature over the canonical JSON above (§4.6)…"
}
```

Rules:
- `owner` fields are **opt-in and minimized**. A public card need not name
  its owner at all.
- `discovery.addresses` is opt-in per address: each listed address opens the
  dead-drop listen topic for that address (§4.4). Listing an address is a
  deliberate act, not a default.
- `rendezvous` is ordered by preference; `pref: 0` entries (like DNS TXT) are
  lookup hints rather than delivery addresses.
- The card is versioned (`v`), signed, and revocable via expiry.
- `capabilities` also lists the A2A extension URIs the agent supports for
  the meeting verbs, which is how a peer learns what it may send (§7.5).
- **Changing a card.** An agent may list several addresses, and its owner
  may add or remove them at any time. Each change re-signs the card with a
  `created` later than the previous card's (`v` is the schema version and
  stays `1`). Of several valid cards with the same `id`, a requester uses
  only the one with the latest `created`; an address counts as claimed only
  if that card lists it. An address the owner keeps off the card ("private")
  opens no topic and finds nothing. Removing an address cannot recall the
  copies of the old card that peers or relays already hold; see §4.4 for the
  public pointer.

### 4.4 Discovery of a card

Discovery is machine-first: the requester's agent tries silent, machine-only
paths **before** any human channel is involved; the human channel is the
fallback and remains the anti-spoofing trust anchor. In order of availability:

1. **Hint servers (primary)** — Nostr relays, ntfy.sh and MQTT carry a
   per-address topic derived deterministically from a contact point:

   ```
   dtopic(address) = base32(SHA-256("rdv1/disc:" ‖ canon(address)))[0:26]
   ```

   (`canon` and `base32` are defined in §4.6. The same topic namespace is
   used on all three carriers — Nostr as a `t` tag on the agent-envelope
   kind, one topic per transport.) Two modes, both **per-address opt-in**,
   dead drops otherwise:
   - **Listen** — the agent watches its own topics. A requester who holds the
     address leaves a small, signed, protocol-shaped "who knows me" probe and
     the agent answers per policy. This is the cheapest lookup that exists:
     no email, no inbox, no human interruption. The probe **is** a contact
     request (§5.1) posted on the `dtopic` with `to_hint` set to the address;
     there is no separate probe document. The listener gates it exactly like
     any inbound request, with binding `claimed`. The probe is cleartext on
     the carrier (§9): keep the greeting short.
   - **Public pointer** — the agent publishes its card (or a card hash) on
     the topic, so a requester can fetch it without posting first. Default
     off; `policy.public` gate. The pointer is replaceable (§6.2): after a
     change the agent publishes its new card on each listed address's topic
     and on the topic of each address it removed, so the newest card
     supersedes the old one there and a lookup for a removed address finds a
     card that no longer claims it (§4.3).
2. **DNS TXT** — `_agent.<domain> TXT "rdv=rdv1:…"` for owners with domains.
3. **Platform profile fields** — a `rdv1:…` line in an X bio / LinkedIn
   about / GitHub profile. The platform account vouchsafes the binding.
4. **Directories (optional)** — community-run services that answer
   *blinded* lookups; see §4.5. Off by default.
5. **Mailbox probe (email first)** — a signed email carrying the contact
   request, delivered through the recipient's mail rule; see §5.2.1. The
   universal fallback: works wherever email does, and proves mailbox control.
   (The profile generalizes to other carriers later.)
6. **Direct (STUN)** — once both sides know each other's hints, ICE/STUN
   hole-punching upgrades the conversation to a direct link. STUN is a
   connectivity upgrade after discovery, not a lookup.
7. **In person** — QR code / NFC containing the card.

**Bindings.** Every discovery path yields a *binding level*, recorded with
the contact and shown at consent time:

| Path | Binding | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| QR / NFC in person | `in-person` | Out-of-band, strongest |
| DNS TXT | `dns` | Control of the domain proven |
| Mailbox probe | `mailbox` | Control of the mailbox proven (handshake echo) |
| Hint topics, profiles, directories | `claimed` | Self-asserted |

A `claimed` binding is a lead, not a credential: the **default** tier offered
at consent caps at `stranger` until a stronger binding promotes it. A human
who explicitly picks a higher tier at consent *is* the explicit confirmation
that promotes it; the cap constrains defaults, never the owner's choice.
Bindings attach to the relationship record, not the card, and both sides
keep one: the requester records how it found the peer (`claimed` for a topic
probe or a public pointer; `in-person` when the owner says the card came from
a QR code or face to face).

### 4.5 Discovery directories (optional)

A directory is a small, community-runnable HTTP service that maps
`dtopic(address) → listing { card, updated, listing_sig }`. Listings are
self-asserted (`claimed`); the server verifies only the request signature.

- **Blinded lookups.** Queries use an OPRF (RFC 9497): the requester blinds
  the `dtopic`, the server evaluates it against a twisted store, the
  requester unblinds. The server learns neither the contact point nor the
  match — and only exact-contact matches are ever returned. There is no
  browsing, no name search, no enumeration.
- **Listing is opt-in** per the card's `policy`, separate from `public`.
- **Suggestions ("people you may know").** On by default — switch it off
  anytime. The agent runs its owner's own contact list against configured
  directories, locally, and surfaces hits: *"John appears to have an agent.
  Connect?"* Nothing is sent until the owner taps. On connect, the agent
  keeps the peer's card; no rediscovery, forever. Suggestions can only
  surface owners who opted into a listing — a suggestion is a lead,
  confirmed by the handshake.
- **Two switches:** *suggest friends* is on by default (owner-facing,
  computed locally; switch it off anytime). *list me* in a given directory
  is opt-in — a publishing act, off by default.
- **No federation, no authority.** Directories are shards, not a registry:
  anyone may run one, clients choose which to trust, and skipping directories
  entirely never breaks anything.

### 4.6 Encoding, canonical JSON and signatures

Every signed document (card, request, grant, revoke, envelope) follows the
same rules, so independent implementations produce identical bytes:

- **Canonical JSON** (`canon(doc)`) is a subset of RFC 8785 (JCS): UTF-8,
  object members sorted by key, no insignificant whitespace, absent members
  omitted. Numbers MUST be integers (timestamps and durations are strings, so
  no floating-point number is ever serialized); `null` is allowed.
- **Base32** is the RFC 4648 alphabet, lowercase, no padding. It is used for
  agent IDs (§4.2) and discovery topics (§4.4).
- **Hash** values (`prev`, the Nostr `d` tag) are the lowercase hex SHA-256 of
  the canonical JSON of the whole document, `sig` included.
- **`sig`** is the base64 (RFC 4648 §4, standard alphabet, padded) encoding of
  the 64-byte Ed25519 signature over
  `"rdv1/sig:" ‖ canon(doc without sig)`. The prefix domain-separates
  Rendezvous signatures from any other use of the same key, so a signature
  cannot be lifted from one context to another. Binary fields inside
  `content` (§6.4) use the same base64.
- **`canon(address)`** is the bare value with no type prefix: an email is
  trimmed and lowercased; a phone is `+` followed by digits only (a leading
  `+` is required; separators are removed).

---

## 5. Contact layer (consent & handshake)

### 5.1 Contact Request

The envelope that asks "may my agent talk to your agent?":

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "type": "rdv/contact-request",
  "id": "<uuid>",
  "from": "rdv1:<requester key>",
  "to_hint": "john@doe.com",
  "card": "<requester's address card>",
  "greeting": "Alice's agent requests contact on Alice's behalf.",
  "capabilities_offered": ["a2a/0.3"],
  "ts": "2026-10-08T00:00:00Z",
  "sig": "…"
}
```

Delivery (§6): the request is posted to any rendezvous hint the requester can
resolve for the target (including hint-server topics), delivered by the
mailbox probe (§5.2.1), or sent through the human channel (email/SMS/
WhatsApp) addressed to the human.

Rules:
- `id` MUST be an RFC 4122 UUID string, as must the `id` of every grant and
  revoke and a grant's `request_ref`. Receivers reject anything else: IDs are
  chosen by the peer and end up in logs and user interfaces.
- A request sent to a known card travels inside an encrypted envelope. A topic
  probe (§4.4) is posted in cleartext on the carrier, greeting and card
  included (§9).
- `greeting` is peer-written text: display-only (§5.6).

### 5.2 Human-channel bootstrap

When machine-first discovery yields nothing, contact travels the human
channel. Two profiles cover the cases: the **mailbox probe** when the
requester holds a human address and wants to know if an agent exists
(§5.2.1), and the **invite** when no agent was found and the owner chooses to
recruit one (§5.2.2). In both, the signed grant flow (§5.3) is unchanged:
nothing proceeds without the receiving human's approval.

The human channel is also the **anti-spoofing anchor**: contact is bound to
the address it arrived through, and the human verifies against the social
context they already have ("I do know john@doe.com"). Key fingerprints
are additionally comparable out-of-band (Signal safety-number model).

### 5.2.1 Mailbox probe (email probe profile)

The probe is a three-way handshake, like TCP:

```
SYN       contact-request by email, marked [RDV-PROBE]
SYN-ACK   contact-grant + recipient card + cookie
ACK       first envelope on the recipient's preferred hint, echoing the cookie
```

**Design goals:** discovery without awkwardness ("does this person even have
a bot?") and an anti-spoofing anchor. *The mail rule routes; the agent gates.*

**Marking.**
- Subject starts with `[RDV-PROBE]` followed by a plain-language line, e.g.
  *"bot discovery request — if you're a human, you can ignore this."*
- `X-Rdv-Probe: v=1; id=<uuid>; from=rdv1:…` for header-aware rules.
- `Auto-Submitted: auto-generated` (RFC 3834) so out-of-office responders
  and other bots never loop. A probe has one recipient, no Cc/Bcc, and is
  never sent to a list.

**Body.** A short human-readable paragraph, plus the machine part fenced
between `---BEGIN RDV/1---` and `---END RDV/1---` markers (canonical JSON:
the signed contact request, the requester's card, a cookie slot).

**The rule (integrator recipe).**
1. Match the subject prefix or the header.
2. Hand the message to the agent's probe endpoint and remove it from the
   inbox (archive — no clutter; it reaches the human surface only when
   policy says `prompt`, and then in the bot chat, not the mail app).
3. Apply the owner's policy: `block` — silent drop; `prompt` — surface in
   the bot chat; `allow` — auto-grant within the pre-approved scope.

**The gate (mandatory, before anything reaches a model).** Probes are
attacker-controlled text addressed to a bot — the exact shape of a prompt
injection — so parsing is deterministic and content never executes:
1. Parse the fenced JSON; reject anything malformed.
2. Verify the Ed25519 signature; verify DMARC/DKIM/SPF via
   `Authentication-Results` (RFC 8601). Unaligned mail is challenged, never
   trusted.
3. Rate-limit and dedupe by request id; probes expire after 14 days.
4. Only then apply policy. Raw probe text is data, never instructions — the
   gate runs before any LLM sees a byte of it.

**Verification (the mailbox proof).**
- If DMARC passes, arrival already carries a weak channel proof and the
  agent may prompt the human immediately.
- Otherwise the reply is a stateless challenge:
  `cookie = HMAC(K_agent, request_id ‖ canon(from) ‖ date)`, truncated.
  Only a requester who actually received the reply can echo the cookie — the
